title: Create a Fresh Database
content:
database.yaml creates an RDS PostgreSQL instance, a subnet group using two private DB subnets and a parameter group requiring TLS. Fresh provisioning creates database tindy with master user tindy_admin, with RDS managing its master password in Secrets Manager. AWS CLI confirmed PostgreSQL 17.11 is available in us-east-1 before this step.
Create the stack Select CloudFormation → Create stack → With new resources (standard) in N. Virginia and upload database.yaml from the infrastructure repository. 📸 Capture the selected filename.
Name the stack tindy-database. Set DBProvisionMode = Fresh, leave DBSnapshotIdentifier empty and keep EnableDeletionProtection = true. Select DatabaseSecurityGroupId and both PrivateDbSubnetIds using Outputs from the newly created Network stack. 📸 Capture the stack name and all parameters.
Add tags Project=Tindy, Environment=tindy, Owner=TindyTeam. Keep Express mode disabled and rollback enabled, review and create the stack. Wait for CREATE_COMPLETE, then record Outputs including the endpoint, port, provision mode and master secret ARN where exported for Fresh. 📸 Capture completed stack status and Outputs.
Bootstrap, migrations and demo seeding take place during Runtime setup before enabling the API. Verify and update the retained API connection secret for the new DB. Verified parameters show stack tindy-database, Fresh provisioning, empty snapshot identifier and enabled deletion protection. Security group and both selected DB subnets match the new Network Outputs. Database creation is complete, with CREATE_COMPLETE and Outputs evidence below.
Verified deployment results Tags, disabled Express mode, rollback and Use deletion policy were configured before reviewing the stack name and template.
Stack tindy-database reached CREATE_COMPLETE with Outputs (5), provisioning mode Fresh, port 5432 and identifier tindy-database-postgres. DBEndpointAddress and DBMasterSecretArn are available for subsequent bootstrap.
📸 The Outputs image also records completed stack status.
The RDS-managed master secret supports bootstrap. The API uses a separate credential through its application connection secret, prepared during Runtime setup. Integrations deployment is next.

title: Tindy architecture overview
content:
Tindy helps users find projects and teammates, manage profiles, apply to projects and communicate with other members. This workshop deploys its AWS frontend, backend, database and PDF scanning infrastructure through six CloudFormation templates.
Objectives Deploy stacks in dependency order, use stack Outputs as subsequent inputs, provision a Fresh database, run bootstrap/migration/seed tasks and verify the application through CloudFront. Seeded data supports the login, project discovery, application and review demonstration.
System architecture The diagram shows the arrangement of service groups and application components.
Component Role CloudFront and frontend S3 Deliver the frontend over HTTPS using Origin Access Control for bucket access. CloudFront VPC Origin and internal ALB Route backend requests from CloudFront to the ECS API. ECS Fargate Run the API and one-off database preparation tasks. RDS PostgreSQL Store application data in private DB subnets with TLS connections. Media S3 Store uploads under application prefixes. GuardDuty, EventBridge and SQS Scan PDFs and deliver results to the API worker, with a DLQ for failed processing. Secrets Manager and SSM Store application secrets and Data Protection keys. ECR and GitHub OIDC Store backend images and support GitHub Actions authentication to AWS. CloudWatch and SNS Provide logs, alarms and email notifications. CloudFormation templates Template Scope foundation.yaml S3, ECR, secrets, OIDC and conditional deployment/operations roles. network.yaml VPC, subnets, routes and security groups. database.yaml RDS instance, subnet group and parameter group. integrations.yaml GuardDuty plan, EventBridge rule, SQS/DLQ, SNS and alarms. edge.yaml CloudFront, Origin Access Control, frontend bucket policy and maintenance routing. runtime.yaml ECS, internal ALB, VPC Origin, IAM roles and task definitions. Practical deployment sequence Clean up the existing environment, documented in section 5.7. Import retained Foundation resources, restore the main template and create Network in section 5.3. Create the Fresh Database and Integrations in section 5.4. Create Edge maintenance to obtain its hostname, provision Runtime with DesiredCount 0, prepare and seed the database, enable the API and switch Edge live in section 5.5. Verify and demonstrate the application in section 5.6. This session uses the existing account in us-east-1, a new CloudFront hostname and newly seeded demo data. Deployment pages record verified results and screenshots as execution proceeds.

title: Blog 1
content:
Kiro Workflows: hand off an issue, get back a reviewed PR on staging Original author Poobalan P Source AWS Builder Center Published Nov 17, 2026 Last modified Nov 17, 2026 1. The Task and the Result Poobalan P describes a workflow that takes a GitHub issue, implements the change, runs two independent reviews, and deploys to staging after the operator approves. The author tested it on an issue to add pagination to a sample notes API. After 51 minutes, the run had produced a draft pull request with tests and two review results. CI passed, and the change reached staging. Merging the PR and releasing to production remain decisions for the development team.
Every issue has different requirements. The path through planning, implementation, testing, review, and staging often stays the same. A recipe captures those steps so the next issue follows the same process. The operator supplies the task and the project’s staging instructions for each run.
2. When to Use Chat or a Workflow Topic Ordinary chat Kiro Workflows Planning Discuss and agree on a plan for the current task. Define the steps and their order in a recipe for reuse. Review Ask for an additional review when needed. Run the two reviews in separate sessions each time the recipe runs. Model selection Choose the model for the active conversation. Set a model and effort level for individual steps. Progress Follow the work in the conversation. Inspect running, paused, and completed steps in the Workflows panel. An ordinary chat suits a quick discussion or a typo fix. A workflow is useful when a recurring review and verification process justifies starting several steps, such as when a team routinely prepares similar changes for staging.
3. The YAML Recipe and Step Handoffs The recipe takes two inputs. issue identifies the GitHub issue, and deploy describes how the project deploys to staging and checks the result. A step can declare an agent, model, prompt, and artifacts for other steps to read. The example below shows a shortened intake step. The author’s repository contains the complete recipe.
name: issue-to-deploy inputs: issue: string deploy: prompt steps: - type: step id: intake agent: wf-planner modelId: qwen3-coder-next artifacts: brief: .kiro/workflow-output/issue-to-deploy/issue.md prompt: > Read GitHub issue {{issue}} and save a short implementation brief. Each step runs in its own session. The plan step needs the issue brief from intake. Reviewers need the diff and the criteria they should check. The verify step needs review results and test commands. Explicit artifact names and locations make those handoffs inspectable.
The Nine Steps from Issue to Staging Step Work Output intake Read the issue and identify its requirements. A brief for the change. plan Plan the implementation and identify the project’s build and test commands. A change plan with verification steps. build Implement the change and add relevant tests. A diff and commit ready for review. code-review Check the behavior, scope, and tests against the issue. Implementation findings. security-review Review the change for security risks. Findings to address before release. gate Combine the reviews and approve only when both reviewers agree. A decision to continue or revise. verify Run checks and prepare the pull request description. Test results, a change summary, and findings worth carrying forward. ship Push the branch, open a draft PR, and wait for CI. A draft pull request and its GitHub checks. deploy Wait for approval, deploy to staging, and run a smoke check. Staging results the operator can verify. The Build–Review Loop and Its Stop Condition The two reviewers run in parallel after build. When either requests a revision, the findings return to the builder for the next round. The workflow pauses for the operator after three rounds without approval. Once both reviewers approve, gate writes APPROVED and the run proceeds.
- type: repeat id: build-and-review maxIterations: 3 onMaxIterations: pause stopCondition: fileCheck: path: .kiro/workflow-output/issue-to-deploy/gate.json jsonPath: verdict value: APPROVED # Full recipe defines the build, parallel reviews, and gate here. The gate file belongs to the active run. If a previous issue left an approval in gate.json, the stop condition could pick it up before the current reviews finish. The author’s plan step resets the state.
send_message severity Outcome success Continue to the next step. warning Pause for a response. The deploy step uses this to request staging approval. error End the run. A CI failure during ship prevents it from reaching the deploy step. 4. What the Sandbox Run Showed The screenshot shows intake, plan, and build complete. Both reviews are in progress in the first loop, with verify, ship, and deploy queued behind them.
Measure reported by the author Sandbox result Total run time 51 minutes Usage About 37.6 credits Code review alone About 37 minutes and 80% of the run’s credits Command approval requests 62 Build–review rounds Both reviewers approved in the first round These figures come from one sandbox run with a particular effort setting. Code review took most of the time. To compare runs, record the effort, wait time, and credit usage of each step. Approval requests also affect how much attention a run needs from the operator.
A reviewer found a missing test but rated it minor, so the workflow continued. The author updated verify to include minor findings in the PR description. The generated summaries also miscounted tests and acceptance criteria. Reviewing the diff, test list, and original issue together exposes gaps that a summary can miss. Sandbox results and lessons from the original article
5. Preparing a Sandbox Run Set up the environment. Use a version of the Kiro IDE with Workflows, a GitHub remote, and an authenticated GitHub CLI. Enable Workflows in Workspace Configuration and open a new chat. Load the recipe. Get issue-to-deploy.workflow.yaml from the author’s repository. Read its prompts, model choices, iteration limit, and deploy step. If you adapt it for another project, check the edited recipe with validate_workflow before running it. Select the repository and issue. For a sandbox, work from your own fork and enable Issues and Actions as needed. Confirm that GitHub CLI targets the fork. Choose an issue with clear acceptance criteria and start from a clean working tree. The issue description becomes part of the prompts, so review the request and intended scope before running it. Supply the inputs. Give the workflow an issue number, the project’s approved staging process, and a check to perform after deployment. The author’s sandbox uses npm run staging as a demonstration step. For a real staging environment, use its deployment command and health endpoint, with access scoped to staging. Review approval requests. Read the action under review. When the run asks to deploy, check the repository, branch, CI state, and review results before making that decision. Example prompt for the sandbox fork:
Run issue-to-deploy for issue 1 in my sandbox fork. Use npm run staging for the staging demonstration. Pause for my approval before that step and record the verification result in the PR description.
6. Verification and Cleanup gh pr view --web gh pr checks cat .kiro/workflow-output/issue-to-deploy/gate.json npm test These checks cover the draft PR, GitHub CI, the gate verdict, and the local tests. After deployment, run a smoke check tied to the issue. For pagination, this could include requesting the first and next pages and checking an out-of-range parameter. Record a response or test log so someone else can verify the result.
When the sandbox run is finished, identify its draft PR, branch, and output files. Close the test PR and remove its branch if they are no longer needed. Save evidence required for review before clearing run artifacts. For a shared staging deployment, follow the team’s runbook to hand over or restore the environment.
References Poobalan P’s article on AWS Builder Center The issue-to-deploy recipe on GitHub Sandbox repository used for the example Kiro Workflows documentation

takeaways Define how an agent will be evaluated before integrating it. The topics of prototyping, deployment, reliability, and security point to a straightforward design question: what is the agent allowed to do, and how will the team verify the result? For an agent that turns input data into a draft, possible checks include content accuracy, error rates, and cases that require human review. Prepare data for its intended use. An AI or analytics workflow depends on knowing which data is authoritative, who may read it, and how it stays current. These questions matter especially when information is spread across systems or exists in several versions. Choose a modernization approach around the problem at hand. The NestJS, .NET, and internal developer platform examples illustrate different starting points. A team can choose an observable problem such as deployment time, manual effort, or difficulty diagnosing failures and use it to evaluate proposed changes. Consider cost and operations during design. S3 storage classes, monitoring for generative AI, and Bedrock spend are examples of decisions that continue after a system goes live. Storage decisions depend on access frequency. For AI workloads, processing volume, latency, and error rates provide a basis for explaining usage and prioritizing improvements. Applying the ideas to work I can use the proposed Tindy architecture to explore three of these topics.
Test each stage of PDF processing. For documents processed through S3, GuardDuty, and Amazon Bedrock, useful test cases include valid files, files awaiting a scan, and extraction results with missing fields. The UI can give users a chance to review and confirm a draft before saving it to their profile. Measure costs against actual usage. Two starting measures are the number of PDF extraction requests and the number of new files per month. For S3, object groups with different access frequencies can be evaluated separately before choosing lifecycle rules. Assess the deployment platform against current needs. The program included several Amazon EKS and GitOps examples. For Tindy’s proposed API on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, deploying a new version, checking task health, and tracing failures are concrete checks to run before evaluating more complex orchestration requirements. HCMC Watch Party experience I attended the FCAJ watch party in Ho Chi Minh City and followed the program streamed from Hanoi. The agenda gave me a sense of the event’s scope and a way to look up technical topics by session code after the event. Agent-assisted software development, S3 storage optimization, and Bedrock cost control are three topics from the catalogue that relate to specific design questions in Tindy.

Module 1 — AWS Cloud and infrastructure fundamentals

title: Blog 2
content:
Multi-Agent Orchestration and Multi-Tenant RAG with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Original author Leonid Gimelshtein Source AWS Builder Center Published Nov 17, 2026 Last modified Nov 17, 2026 This architecture connects an orchestrator, specialist agents, and Code Interpreter to a retrieval tool behind AgentCore Gateway. Cedar evaluates who can invoke the tool. Metadata filters limit the documents that can be returned to the tenant and permissions of the user who initiated the request.
1. The Multi-Tenant RAG Problem In a retrieval-augmented generation application, the system retrieves relevant document passages before it sends context to the model. When several organizations share the application and document collection, each organization has its own tenant. Two users from different tenants can ask the same question and receive answers grounded in different documents. Users within one tenant can also have different access based on ownership, group sharing, and visibility.
Multi-agent orchestration creates additional points where document content moves. A request may pass through retrieval, two analyses, a calculation, and report generation. At each boundary, the application needs to identify who coordinates the work, who can invoke the retrieval tool, and what context each agent can receive.
2. One Orchestrator Owns the Request Component Responsibility Next.js backend Verify the user session and determine access scope from trusted application data. Orchestrator Retrieve context, delegate tasks, collect results, and assemble the final response. Agent A and Agent B Accept a focused task and relevant document passages, then return structured results. Interpreter agent Invoke AgentCore Code Interpreter when a calculation or data transformation is needed. AgentCore Gateway and Cedar Authenticate the caller and evaluate permission to invoke the knowledge-base tool under the deployed policy. Knowledge-base tool Construct the filtered retrieval request from verified scope. Bedrock Knowledge Bases and OpenSearch Serverless Run retrieval using the vector index in this architecture. Amazon S3 Store source documents and generated artifacts when the workflow persists them. Suppose a user asks for a summary of QA findings and the proportion in each severity category. The orchestrator retrieves context within the user’s authorized scope. It can ask Agent A to summarize findings and Agent B to extract classification criteria. Both tasks can run in parallel. Once they return, the orchestrator can send selected structured data to the interpreter for the calculation and assemble the final response.
Separate Runtimes and Focused Permissions The example can host the orchestrator and specialists in separate AgentCore Runtimes, using the Strands SDK and Claude on Amazon Bedrock. Each runtime can have its own execution role and tool set. Agent A and Agent B receive the retrieved passages from the orchestrator. Direct access to the knowledge base or permission to write reports is granted only where a specialist task requires it.
The interpreter agent decides what calculation or transformation to perform. Code Interpreter executes it in the processing session. The orchestrator can skip this step for tasks that only need text analysis. Intermediate files and results remain within the scope of the original request.
3. The Tool Invocation and Retrieval Boundaries Retrieval path Orchestrator → AgentCore Gateway → Cedar → knowledge-base tool → Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Control Question Result Gateway policy May the authenticated caller invoke this tool for this request? With enforcement enabled, a denied request stops before the tool runs. Metadata filter built by the tool Which documents may this user read in the current tenant? The Knowledge Base receives a query with metadata conditions and returns matching passages. Permission to invoke the tool allows the request to proceed to the document access check. The tool still needs to obtain tenant, user, and document permissions from server-verified data or an authenticated context. Keeping retrieval behind this interface gives the team a defined place to enforce the filter. AgentCore’s ENFORCE mode applies policy decisions, while LOG_ONLY records them for observation. AgentCore policy enforcement modes
4. Identity Follows the Request Cognito authenticates the user. The Next.js backend validates the token used by its session, including signature, issuer, expiry, and applicable token type and client checks. It resolves tenant membership, user ID, and groups from a trusted source. Service identity authorizes runtime calls. IAM can authorize the backend to invoke the runtime and grant each workload the AWS permissions it needs. Runtime permissions and the user’s document access are evaluated at their respective boundaries. The Gateway receives end-user identity. In this JWT-based design, the orchestrator passes the appropriate access token through the authentication channel. Prompts contain the task and authorized context. The server manages tokens and authorization values. The tool builds the filter from trusted scope. Agent-generated query text describes what to find. Server logic verifies the tenant, user ID, and groups that determine what can be returned. Retrieval stops if the trusted scope is missing. If the Gateway policy needs tenantId, inspect the access token actually issued to the Gateway. A tenant attribute in an ID token does not automatically appear in the access token. AWS documents access-token customization through a pre-token generation trigger for supported Cognito configurations. Customizing Amazon Cognito access tokens
5. An Illustrative Cedar Policy Binds the Tenant This policy illustrates a Gateway with a JWT authorizer. It evaluates an OAuth principal, a specific tool action and Gateway, and the match between the input tenant and the verified claim.
permit ( principal is AgentCore::OAuthUser, action == AgentCore::Action::"kb-tool___queryKnowledgeBase", resource == AgentCore::Gateway::"<gateway-arn>" ) when { principal.hasTag("tenantId") && principal.getTag("tenantId") != "" && context.input.tenantId == principal.getTag("tenantId") }; hasTag checks for the claim before getTag reads it. The sample uses context.input.tenantId for the tenant field supplied to the tool. In a deployment, use the Gateway’s action name and ARN, confirm the input schema, and check the claims issued by the application. Principal-scoped policies · Policy in AgentCore
This condition binds one tool call to the caller’s tenant. Trusted application logic still determines ownership, groups, and administrative permissions. Where several policies apply, verify the combined authorization decision and keep the tenant condition mandatory in the retrieval tool.
6. Filter Metadata Before Context Reaches Agents On ingestion, the application assigns tenantId and ownerId from trusted identity. allowedGroups lists the groups permitted to read the document in that tenant. visibility can represent sharing allowed by the application’s policy. Metadata and document permissions need to stay in sync when access changes.
The example below uses tenant-a, user-123, and the qa group. The Knowledge Base can return passages from documents in tenant-a that the user owns or that are shared with the verified group.
{ "andAll": [ { "equals": { "key": "tenantId", "value": "tenant-a" } }, { "orAll": [ { "equals": { "key": "ownerId", "value": "user-123" } }, { "listContains": { "key": "allowedGroups", "value": "qa" } } ] } ] } The outer andAll requires a tenant match and a match in at least one branch of orAll. listContains checks whether the metadata list contains the specified value. A document in another tenant with the same qa group value fails the outer tenant condition. For multiple verified groups, the tool can add one branch per group. If only one access condition applies, include it directly in andAll, because orAll requires at least two entries. The ingestion and retrieval paths need to account for missing required metadata. Bedrock RetrievalFilter · Configuring Knowledge Base queries
Once retrieval finishes, the orchestrator can distribute the returned passages by task. An analyst may need a subset on a particular topic, while the interpreter may only need an extracted table. Each step receives the material required for its part of the request.
7. Tenant Scope After Retrieval Derived data How the application preserves scope Conversation history Resolve a saved or resumed session using the appropriate tenant and identity. Retrieval and response caches Partition by tenant and the relevant access scope. Account for permission changes when refreshing or invalidating entries. Interpreter files Bind sessions and storage locations to the request. Limit inputs to the files needed for the calculation. Reports and exported files Associate results with the tenant and access policy. Check current permission before returning a saved artifact. Logs and traces Record request identifiers and decision points for investigation. Keep access tokens and document contents out of operational logs. The supplied write-up reports two findings for the scenarios it covered. Unauthorized requests were rejected, and retrieval stayed within the user’s permitted scope. The following example checks show which boundary to inspect for each expected result.
Verification case Expected evidence An authorized caller owns a document in the tenant The Gateway permits the tool call. The tool sends a filter and the returned context can include eligible passages. A user belongs to a group with document access The filter uses the verified group and can return matching documents within the tenant. The shared index contains a document from another tenant Its content is absent from retrieval results, specialist context, and reports for the active tenant. The tenant scope is unverified The request stops before retrieval. The application does not run an unfiltered search. A user opens a saved report The application checks the tenant and current read permission before returning the artifact. 8. Putting the Architecture Together Cognito and Next.js establish end-user identity. An orchestrator coordinates AgentCore Runtimes where the Strands SDK defines agent behavior and Claude on Bedrock performs analysis. Gateway and Cedar control access to the knowledge-base tool, which supplies mandatory tenant filtering for Bedrock Knowledge Bases and OpenSearch Serverless. Amazon S3 holds source documents and retained artifacts. Code Interpreter handles computation when needed. AWS CDK describes the infrastructure for repeatable deployments.
When adding a specialist or changing how a report is calculated, the team can trace the request back to its authenticated caller, the policy decision, and the filtered passages supplied to the agents. Those records give the team concrete places to verify access as the workflow evolves.

title: Proposal
content:
Tindy — An AWS Platform for Finding Projects and Teammates 1. Executive Summary Tindy is a web application that helps students and early-career professionals find projects that fit their skills and availability. Project leads publish openings for specific positions, track applications, and send invitations. Once a candidate is accepted, Tindy updates project membership and the position’s filled seats so both users see the same state.
The proposed demo runs in US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1. CloudFront serves the React frontend from S3 and sends dynamic requests to the ASP.NET Core API on ECS Fargate. The API stores business data in RDS for PostgreSQL. The private media bucket stores documents, while GuardDuty scans PDFs and Amazon Bedrock drafts profile suggestions.
2. Problem and Scope Problem Recruiting information is often spread across chat groups, posts, and forms. Applicants struggle to see which positions are open, which skills they require, and how many hours they expect each week. Leads must ask for the same information again and track applications, invitations, and open seats across channels. Tindy brings this information together for each project and position.
Demo Scope Workflow User action Result in Tindy Build a profile A member completes onboarding and enters skills, preferred role, experience, and availability. Eligible text or CV PDF input can be used to generate a draft. The profile is updated after its owner reviews and saves it. Apply to a position A lead publishes an open position. A member discovers the project, selects a position, and confirms the application. The lead reviews the submission. The submitted application is Pending. Once accepted, the member appears in the project and the position’s filled-seat count increases. Invite a teammate A lead selects a project and position, finds a candidate who has opted in, and sends an invitation. The candidate opens the notification and responds. The invitation is Pending until resolved. When the candidate accepts and the API verifies eligibility, the application creates a membership and updates the seat count. Communicate Members exchange direct messages or join a project conversation where they have permission. Authorized users see new messages in the correct conversation. Operate the demo The operator releases the frontend and API, checks service health, backs up data, and rebuilds the environment if needed. Release details, verification results, and backup references support recovery. Interpreting Match Scores The API scores each position using four base weights: required skills 40%, preferred role 30%, availability 20%, and optional skills 10%. If a position has no skills in a category or availability cannot be calculated, the API normalizes the remaining applicable weights. A missing preferred role contributes zero for that criterion.
For example, a candidate who matches all required and optional skills and the preferred role, and can contribute 5 of the 10 hours per week the project needs, scores 90/100. The score explains fit. Users make recruitment decisions and the API rechecks permission, project state, and capacity when processing acceptance.
Benefits and How to Evaluate Them For members, discovery exposes the position being recruited for, expected weekly hours, and any missing skills. A profile can be reused across positions. For project leads, applications and invitations are organized by project and position. When recruiting succeeds, the application state, project membership, and filled-seat count can be checked against the same business records.
The trial will measure the value of these workflows. For recruitment, record the steps and elapsed time from selecting a position to both parties confirming its outcome. For profile entry, use the same sample information to compare manual entry with drafting, reviewing, and correcting AI suggestions. Infrastructure cost, demo setup time, and the effort needed to review suggestions inform the evaluation. These measurements support an assessment of value after the trial.
3. Solution Architecture Tindy architecture diagram for the proposal. The numbered walkthrough below reflects the repository configuration and application code.
Step Component Request or data flow 1 Amazon CloudFront and frontend S3 bucket Users open the site over HTTPS. CloudFront serves the React/Vite build from a private S3 bucket. Origin Access Control (OAC) restricts frontend reads to the distribution. 2 CloudFront VPC Origin and Application Load Balancer Dynamic paths such as /api/*, /hubs/*, and sign-in callbacks reach an internal ALB. The web app and API share a hostname, and caching is disabled for these dynamic paths. CloudFront VPC origins 3 Amazon ECS, AWS Fargate, and Amazon ECR ECS runs the ASP.NET Core .NET 10 API container from ECR. The API handles authentication, profiles, discovery, recruitment, and SignalR chat. ALB health checks track task health. 4 Media S3 bucket, GuardDuty, EventBridge, and SQS A private bucket stores media. Certificate and AI input PDFs go through the scanning workflow. EventBridge routes GuardDuty verdicts to SQS so a worker can update document status. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) holds failed messages for investigation. 5 Amazon Bedrock For AI input PDFs, the backend verifies a clean scan verdict for the corresponding S3 object before allowing extraction. Users can also submit text. The backend validates the output and returns draft profile fields, skills, experience, certificates, and warnings for review. 6 Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL PostgreSQL 17 stores structured data such as accounts, profiles, projects, positions, applications, invitations, and messages. RDS uses private subnets, requires TLS, and restricts access through security groups. Three Flows Through the Diagram Application access and data updates (1 → 2 → 3 → 6). The browser loads the frontend from S3 through CloudFront. When users open projects, apply, or connect to chat, CloudFront routes the dynamic request through the VPC origin to the internal ALB. The ALB selects a healthy Fargate task. The API verifies the JWT and permissions for the project or conversation before reading from or writing to PostgreSQL. Web, API, and chat share a hostname.
Certificate upload and PDF checks (3 → 4). The API receives media and writes the PDF to private S3 storage. GuardDuty scans the file, EventBridge routes the verdict to SQS, and a worker matches it with the S3 object or version and updates document status. The API blocks reads or extraction that require a clean verdict while the document is pending or ineligible. The DLQ holds messages that fail processing after the configured retries.
Profile extraction (4 → 5 → 3 → 6). An AI input PDF can proceed to extraction after a clean scan. Users can also submit text directly. The backend calls Bedrock, validates the response, and returns draft profile fields, skills, experience, and certificates. The API writes the selected fields to PostgreSQL after the user reviews, edits, and confirms the save.
Networking and availability. The VPC spans two Availability Zones. The ALB is internal. Fargate tasks use public subnets and receive public IPv4 addresses in the current configuration. Security groups restrict API ingress to the ALB. The demo runbook uses one Fargate task, and the database template configures Single-AZ RDS. The two zones in the diagram show subnet placement. Scaling out requires verification of SignalR across tasks and background event processing.
Security and operations. Frontend assets and media use separate S3 buckets. The backend authenticates users with JWTs and enforces resource-level permissions. Secrets Manager holds connection details and sensitive configuration. GitHub Actions assumes deployment roles through OIDC. CloudWatch collects logs and monitors target health, HTTP 5xx responses, and the DLQ. SNS delivers alerts when notifications are configured.
Components and Design Rationale Layer Responsibility in the demo Why this design fits Web React and Vite produce static assets. CloudFront reads from S3 through Origin Access Control and serves application routes. The frontend can be released independently. Static assets and dynamic session data use separate cache behaviors. API ASP.NET Core runs in ECS Fargate. ECR stores release images. The ALB checks readiness and routes traffic to healthy tasks. The active release can be traced to an image digest, and a new revision can be checked during rollout. Business data RDS for PostgreSQL stores profiles, project relationships, recruitment states, and chat history. Relationships among projects, positions, and members can be checked when the application writes data. Migrations manage schema changes alongside application releases. Files and events The private media bucket stores files. GuardDuty scans PDFs, EventBridge delivers scan events, and the SQS consumer updates document state. Upload and scan completion happen at different times. The queue exposes pending work and the DLQ provides a place to inspect failures. AI When enabled, the backend calls Bedrock and returns a structured draft. Users can compare suggestions with source material. The backend validates profile fields and skill and role mappings before review. Data Boundaries, Access, and Observability Data placement. PostgreSQL stores identities, profiles, project relationships, and workflow states. The frontend S3 bucket contains HTML and static bundles. The media S3 bucket contains file content. A recovery manifest needs both the RDS snapshot reference and the relevant S3 object references so the team can verify that restored records still resolve to the corresponding files.
Access by layer. Security groups govern network access among the ALB, API tasks, and database. The backend authenticates the user and authorizes access to the relevant project, profile, or conversation. The ECS execution role supports startup operations such as pulling the image, initializing logging, and resolving configured secrets. The ECS task role covers AWS actions needed by application code, such as media access, scan-result processing, and AI calls when enabled. The OIDC permissions used by GitHub Actions for releases are managed independently of runtime permissions.
Operational signals. Target health and 5xx responses help narrow down whether a problem is in routing or the application. ECS events and CloudWatch Logs show whether a task could start, stopped, or returned an error. For PDFs, correlate the document state in Tindy with the GuardDuty result and pending SQS or DLQ messages. Recruitment notifications appear in the application through API polling. Chat uses SignalR. SNS serves operational alerts when configured.
Demo Trade-offs and What Would Justify Scaling Decision What the demo prioritizes Evidence needed for a change One Fargate task behind the ALB Keep the always-running footprint small and simplify real-time chat for the demo. Measure traffic and latency. Verify SignalR event delivery across tasks and check that background event processing remains consistent before increasing task count. Single-AZ RDS Keep the starting configuration simple and preserve a documented snapshot recovery path. Define acceptable downtime and data loss. Estimate the cost of Multi-AZ and rehearse recovery before committing to higher availability. API tasks in public subnets with ingress through an internal ALB Use the existing outbound path for integrations. Security groups restrict access to the API. Before moving to private subnets, inventory AWS and external destinations and compare endpoints and outbound paths for connectivity, cost, and operating effort. On-demand AI extraction Process inputs when a user requests a draft and make the run time and cost per attempt measurable. Measure invalid outputs, latency, and token use before considering a background processing queue. 4. Implementation and Testing Prepare the Infrastructure and Data AWS CloudFormation defines six stacks: foundation, network, database, integrations, runtime, and edge. Foundation and network provide buckets, ECR, IAM, and networking. Database provides PostgreSQL. Integrations handles PDF scan results. Runtime deploys the API, ALB, and VPC origin. Edge uses that origin to route dynamic requests once the service is ready.
Choose Fresh to create a database, apply migrations, and seed demo data, or Restore to recover schema and data from a snapshot. For a release that changes the schema, take a snapshot first and run the EF Core migration in a separate ECS task. Verify the running API remains compatible with the migrated schema so the API can return to the previous revision if rollout fails.
Release the Application After CI passes, select the approved commit. Build the backend image, push it to ECR, and record the image digest used in the ECS task definition. Verify the ECS service is stable and ALB targets are healthy. With the edge in live mode, check that /api/health/ready returns HTTP 200 with status Healthy through CloudFront. Build the frontend with Vite, publish it to S3, and invalidate the CloudFront cache. Check the home page, login page, and JavaScript bundle through the same hostname. Run acceptance scenarios with sample accounts and PDFs. Record the commit, image digest, ECS revision, test results, and snapshot ID where applicable. When rebuilding the demo, keep the edge in maintenance mode until the API, database, and required integrations are ready. Technical and Non-Functional Requirements Release environment. The application uses React/Vite, ASP.NET Core .NET 10, EF Core, and PostgreSQL. Build the frontend to use same-origin API paths. Supply environment settings and sensitive configuration through the deployment workflow and AWS Secrets Manager. Consistency. Membership admission must use the current project and position state. Check both membership and the position’s filled-seat count after acceptance and reload. Privacy. Use test accounts and sample documents for demonstrations. Verify permissions when opening a document, requesting an AI draft, or accessing a conversation. Keep references and status evidence in test records. Keep secret values and résumé contents out of those records. Testability. Prepare test data for successful actions and for rejected actions. Include a position with no open seats, a candidate who has not opted in, a PDF with a pending scan, and a user who lacks conversation access. Recoverability. Record the relevant snapshot and version before schema changes. Identify a sample set of application records and media files to reconcile after Restore. Lifecycle Between Demonstrations After a demo, check whether application writes or PDF scan work are still in progress. Once the environment is ready for backup, record the snapshot ID, timestamp, encryption status, API release, and current migration. Confirm that the S3 objects and ECR image needed by that recovery point are retained.
If the environment is taken down between demos, switch CloudFront to maintenance and verify that the distribution hostname is retained. The project runbook defines checks before removing runtime, database, and integrations in dependency order. Preserve the agreed recovery resources, including the snapshot, S3 data, ECR image, and configuration references. At the next demo, select Restore or Fresh based on the goal, verify the database endpoint and health checks, and reopen the edge when the required services are ready.
5. Sprint Plan and Deployment Milestones Tindy development begins on Monday, October 5, 2026 (Week 4). The plan groups Weeks 4–9 into three two-week development sprints. Week 10 (November 16–22, 2026) is reserved for deployment to AWS, post-deployment verification, and completion of the demo.
Sprint Dates Main work End-of-sprint deliverable Sprint 1 · Application foundation Weeks 4–5 · October 5–18, 2026 Start development. Agree on user flows and the data model. Set up React/Vite, ASP.NET Core, and PostgreSQL. Build sign-in, onboarding, profiles, and the skill and role catalogs. A sample user can sign in, complete onboarding, and save a profile through the API. Sprint 2 · Projects and recruiting Weeks 6–7 · October 19–November 1, 2026 Build project and position management, project discovery, match scoring, applications, teammate discovery, and invitations. Recheck recruitment eligibility and capacity at acceptance. Sample data demonstrates the application and invitation flows. Successful acceptance updates project membership and filled seats correctly. Sprint 3 · Integrations and release preparation Weeks 8–9 · November 2–15, 2026 Complete SignalR chat and in-app notifications. Integrate file storage, PDF scanning, and Bedrock profile drafts. Prepare CloudFormation templates, CI/CD configuration, and demo data. A release candidate, test scenarios for core workflows, and reviewed AWS configuration. Sprint 4 · Deployment and completion Week 10 · November 16–22, 2026 Deploy the frontend and API to AWS. Check CloudFront, the ALB, ECS, and RDS. Run acceptance scenarios through the demo hostname, resolve issues affecting core workflows, and record release details. A deployed AWS demo with API readiness returning HTTP 200 and status Healthy, acceptance results, and redeployment instructions. The project completion milestone is in Week 10. From Week 11 through the December 14, 2026 internship wrap-up, reporting work covers the architecture diagram, demo scenarios, acceptance results, release details, and cost assumptions.
6. Budget Estimate The always-on scenario runs for 730 hours per month in us-east-1. The figures come from the Tindy-Always-on workload estimate exported from AWS Pricing Calculator on November 18, 2026, using rates before discounts and excluding taxes and credits.
Cost item Basis Reference cost AWS Fargate One Linux/x86 task with 0.5 vCPU and 2 GiB RAM. The estimate includes 365 vCPU-hours and 1,460 GB-hours of memory. USD 21.26/month Application Load Balancer One internal ALB for 730 hours. USD 16.43/month Public IPv4 One in-use public IPv4 address for the task for 730 hours. USD 3.65/month RDS for PostgreSQL One Single-AZ db.t4g.micro for 730 hours (USD 11.68) and 20 GiB gp3 (USD 2.30). USD 13.98/month Edge, media, security, and AI CloudFront, S3, ECR, Secrets Manager, GuardDuty, EventBridge, SQS, CloudWatch, and Bedrock. Charges vary with storage, requests, logs, scans, and tokens. Usage-based The always-on baseline is USD 55.32 per month. The baseline excludes ALB LCUs, any RDS CPU credit charges and additional backup or snapshot storage, and the usage-based services listed above. Include retained snapshots and other retained resources when estimating the scheduled demo scenario. AWS Pricing Calculator
The public estimate displays USD 55.34 per month. Compared with the AWS Console export, the displayed Fargate and ALB costs are each USD 0.01 higher. The public ALB calculation uses 0.001 GB/hour of assumed traffic because the form requires a positive LCU input.
At pilot traffic, budget about USD 58 per month for always-on infrastructure and the modeled supporting services. The Cost Explorer export for November 1–17, 2026 shows core infrastructure activity concentrated on November 11–17. Treat that week as representative of a 30-day month. Add USD 1.60 for four stored secrets and scale the other imported usage priced in AWS Pricing Calculator (USD 0.1804 × 30/7, including Secrets Manager API calls). This planning figure excludes ALB LCUs, unverified EventBridge charges, RDS CPU credits, additional backup or snapshot storage, and taxes.
Comparing Operating Scenarios Cost input Always-on scenario Scheduled demo scenario Fargate and public IPv4 Model runtime against the 730-hour reference month. Count actual task hours, including setup and verification before each demo. ALB and RDS Count the hours the ALB and database are provisioned or running and add configuration-dependent charges. Record ALB lifetime, database runtime, and snapshot storage kept between demos separately. Retained storage and configuration Measure S3 and ECR storage, backups, and retained configuration items. Include resources retained for recovery while the edge is in maintenance. Traffic, scanning, and AI Use a defined baseline for requests, downloads, scans, and tokens. Measure activity per session and record repeat processing. Hold usage assumptions constant when comparing runtime costs. After the trial, compare per-service billing with the amount of time resources remained provisioned. Classify differences as runtime, storage, traffic, or document processing. AWS Budgets can alert at an agreed threshold, while Cost Explorer provides a breakdown for investigating the source of a variance.
7. Risk Assessment Risk Impact Mitigation API or database interruption in the demo configuration Users temporarily lose access to application workflows. Monitor readiness, ECS logs, and ALB health. Define snapshot recovery procedures and acceptable downtime. PDF rejection, failed scan, or slow processing A certificate or CV cannot yet be used. Show scan status, block reads and extraction until eligibility is met, monitor the DLQ, and verify the corresponding S3 object. Incomplete or incorrect AI suggestions Incorrect information could enter a profile if unreviewed. Validate the output structure and skill catalog mappings, then require user review and allow corrections before saving. Migration or release mismatch Web, API, and database schema versions can become incompatible. Take a snapshot before changes, release in a compatible order, and record the commit, digest, and revision for recovery. Resources continue accruing charges after the demo ALB, compute, database, logs, or snapshots may continue billing. Track the budget, identify retained resources, and review billing after cleanup. Incident Triage and Recovery Identify the affected path. Check API readiness, ALB target health, and ECS first. If the web and API are reachable and only PDF processing fails, inspect document state, the scan result, and the queue independently. Preserve evidence and recovery options. Record the time, revision, image digest, and most recent change. For a suspected rollout failure, verify schema compatibility before attempting to return to an earlier API revision. Confirm recovery with sample data. When restoring RDS, select the intended snapshot and verify TLS connectivity, database permissions, sample records, and linked S3 media. Compare the snapshot time with the last valid update to identify changes that need reconciliation. Reopen when checks pass. Use readiness and the core workflow tests to decide when to return CloudFront to live. Record the cause, how the issue was detected, and any runbook step to update. 8. Expected Outcomes and Acceptance Criteria Acceptance scenario How to test Expected evidence Member submits an application Use a recruiting position with an open seat. Submit an application as a member and accept it as the project lead. The application moves from Pending to Accepted. The member appears in the project, the position’s filled-seat count increases once, and the data remains consistent after reloading. Project lead invites a teammate Use separate test data. The candidate opts in, the lead sends an invitation, and the candidate opens the notification and accepts. The invitation identifies the correct project and position. The seat count stays the same while the invitation is pending and updates after successful acceptance. Chat through CloudFront Open two signed-in sessions with access to the same conversation and send a message from one session. The other session receives it in the correct conversation. DevTools records the WebSocket upgrade with status 101. PDF scanning Upload a sample certificate or AI input PDF. Track the scan state from pending to verdict. Actions requiring a clean verdict remain blocked while the scan is pending. A clean verdict for the matching S3 object or version makes the document eligible for its intended use. AI profile draft Submit text or a scanned and eligible PDF, review the suggested fields, make edits, and confirm save. Suggestions are structured and warnings identify missing or conflicting data. The saved profile reflects the fields the user confirmed. Release and recovery Open the site through CloudFront, check API readiness and core workflows, then rebuild a test environment from a selected snapshot using the runbook. Web and API share a hostname, readiness returns 200 and Healthy, and sample data matches the recovery point. Release details, snapshot ID, and reconciliation results are recorded. Handover Evidence For each acceptance run, record the environment and version, the action performed, the expected result, and what was observed. Use sample accounts for recruitment and record the before-and-after states. For releases, capture the commit, image digest, readiness result, and snapshot reference. For PDF and AI checks, use sample documents and retain the scan state and an example reviewed draft. This lets a reader verify the result without access to an individual’s account or personal data.
Technical basis. See the templates in tindy-infrastructure/cloudformation, the Tindy release and redeployment runbooks, DISCOVERY_PROJECT_FLOW.md, TEAMMATE_FLOW.md, AI_PROFILE_EXTRACTION.md, and the backend chat documentation.

title: Foundation and Network
content:
Build Tindy storage, application configuration and networking. Foundation supplies buckets, the image registry and secret references. Network provides the VPC, subnets and security groups used by Database and Runtime.
This session follows cleanup. Nine Foundation resources were retained, so import them into the new stack before restoring the main template.
5.3.1 — Deploy Foundation foundation.yaml manages persistent resources and conditional GitHub Actions roles.
Resource group Purpose in Tindy Frontend bucket Stores frontend build assets, served by CloudFront using Origin Access Control. Media bucket and policy Store uploads and enforce access conditions used by PDF scanning. ECR repository Stores API images, pinned by digest for Runtime. Application secrets Provide DB, JWT and OAuth configuration references to ECS tasks. GitHub OIDC provider Supports GitHub Actions authentication through deployment roles. Deployment/operations IAM roles Grant permissions to workflows when their parameters enable them. First, import nine retained resources with foundation-import.yaml. After IMPORT_COMPLETE, update with foundation.yaml to restore Outputs and recreate InfraPlannerRole. Configure roles that depend on new CloudFront and Runtime inputs when those inputs are available.

5.3.2 — Deploy Network network.yaml creates VPC 10.20.0.0/16. Each subnet group spans two Availability Zones and serves a specific component.
Component Use Public task subnets Fargate API and one-off tasks with public IP assignment configured in ECS. Private app subnets Internal ALB, connected to CloudFront through a VPC Origin. Private DB subnets RDS PostgreSQL subnet group. Internet Gateway and route tables Routing for the subnet groups. Security groups and ingress rules Control traffic between ALB, API, migration tasks and the database. The template defines 26 resources and nine Outputs. Use the new networking IDs in sections 5.4 and 5.5. Subnets span two Availability Zones, while API task count and database Multi-AZ behavior follow Runtime and Database settings.

title: Blog 3
content:
AWS Emulator: First Impressions From a Real Serverless App Original author Ran Isenberg Source Ran The Builder Published Nov 12, 2026 Last modified Nov 13, 2026 Ran Isenberg experimented with moving integration tests for the AWS Lambda Handler Cookbook from deployed AWS resources to AWS Emulator. The first full run reported 34 passing integration tests in about seven seconds. The Lambda application code and individual test bodies stayed the same. The main changes involved starting the test environment, setting the SDK endpoint, and adapting the test setup around behavior the tested emulator build handled differently. Original article and experiment results
1. The Serverless Testing Pyramid Before the Change The previous workflow used an ephemeral stack, a temporary deployment in an AWS test account that could be created for a branch. Unit tests and infrastructure definition checks ran locally. Developers could launch integration tests from their IDE, but those tests still called services from the deployed stack. End-to-end tests exercised the deployed application along the path a client would use.
This approach gives developers feedback from the AWS services themselves. It also adds a deployment or update before branch-level integration testing. Giving an AI coding agent the ability to run those tests raises a second question about where deployment credentials should live. The author’s goal was to keep the edit-and-test loop local while leaving access to the AWS account in a controlled delivery pipeline.
Mocks already had a place in the old workflow. They helped make a particular dependency fail on demand so a test could check the application’s response. Isenberg also describes using Moto for a case that needed a simulated organization with 10,000 accounts. Different tools are useful depending on what a particular test needs to prove. The author’s testing approach
2. Where AWS Emulator Sits in the Test Process AWS Emulator exposes a local endpoint that implements AWS APIs for development and testing. AWS documents native Linux packages and a Docker path for Windows, macOS, and other supported setups. In this example, pytest still runs the handler in its own process. The SDK uses AWS_ENDPOINT_URL to route the relevant requests to the emulator, which maintains resource state for the run. AWS Emulator User Guide
Call the handler with a test event. The handler executes the application logic and data-access layer used by the service. Return mocked results inside the test process. A fixture can supply an AppConfig feature flag or another deliberately fixed dependency response. Send SDK requests to the local endpoint. The diagram uses https://127.0.0.1:9297. A DynamoDB write and a later read can use the same emulated table. Check the response and the stored state. An order creation case can inspect the handler’s response and read back the order. A repeated-request case can check that the application handles the same request without creating an unexpected second order. The local test job uses emulator credentials when request signing is required and configures its SDK to trust the emulator’s CA. Real AWS credentials stay outside the job. The setup checks the effective endpoint before running tests and stops on a missing or unexpected configuration. This is especially useful when an SDK client has its own endpoint settings. Pointing an AWS SDK at AWS Emulator
3. Moving Integration Tests Before Deployment Test layer Where it runs in the revised setup What it covers Unit Local or CI Business rules, input validation, and logic isolated from services. Infrastructure Local or CI before deployment Expectations about declared resources and values in the infrastructure definition. Integration Local or CI with the emulator and selective mocks The handler, SDK, and emulated resources working together within the test’s scope. End-to-end A test stack on AWS API Gateway reaching Lambda, real identity integration, IAM roles and policies, and deployed configuration. A developer or coding agent can update code, run unit and integration tests, and open a pull request from an environment without AWS account access. CI repeats linting, type checks, unit tests, and emulator integration tests. After approval, the deployment job uses scoped AWS permissions to create the test stack, run end-to-end checks, and remove temporary resources from that run.
The CI/CD permissions establish this separation. Pointing an SDK at loopback changes where its configured requests go. The integration job’s identity still determines whether it could reach real AWS through another path. AWS also documents that IAM and resource policy evaluation in the emulator differs from AWS. IAM and deployed security checks therefore belong on a controlled AWS test stack. AWS Emulator limitations
4. What the AWS Lambda Handler Cookbook Experiment Covered The sample Python service lets a client sign in and call API Gateway to create, retrieve, list, or delete orders. Lambda validates requests and runs the business logic. One DynamoDB table stores orders. The other supports idempotency through Powertools. Cognito issues user tokens, AppConfig supplies runtime feature flags, and AWS CDK defines the deployed stack. AWS Lambda Handler Cookbook
The migration added a Makefile path for starting the emulator locally and made the emulator a CI dependency. The integration job moved before deployment and checked its endpoint to avoid using a live AWS account. The first full run passed 34 integration tests in roughly seven seconds. This is a measurement of the author’s suite and environment. In a different project, measure emulator startup, test data preparation, and test execution separately when making a comparison. Original article · Migration pull request
Component Treatment in the reported experiment What the result covers DynamoDB The handler uses the SDK to call the emulated tables. Order persistence and the Powertools idempotency store exercised by the suite. Lambda and API Gateway pytest builds sample events and invokes Python handlers directly. Handler logic and its dependencies. The deployed API Gateway-to-Lambda path belongs to E2E. AppConfig The existing mock stays in the suite. Application behavior for feature-flag values provided by the fixtures. Cognito The local suite uses test-only tokens suited to its application scenarios. The local authentication path exercised by the fixtures. Live signing-key retrieval and user pool behavior remain checks for AWS E2E. The distinction matters when interpreting the reported result. The local suite exercised the handlers, order data, and idempotency together. It did not exercise the emulator’s own Lambda or API Gateway implementation. The deployed suite verifies the wiring that sits outside the in-process test.
5. Four Approaches When an API Behaves Differently Approach When it helps What the team takes on Deploy a test stack to AWS The test depends on live IAM, deployed configuration, or cross-service behavior. Deployment time, resource cost, and management of test account access. Mock calls in-process The test needs a deliberate failure or needs to isolate application logic. Mock responses need maintenance when service contracts or assumptions change. Use the emulator with small workarounds Most required APIs behave as expected and the remaining gaps can be isolated with fixtures. Document the behavior each workaround leaves to E2E and recheck it after upgrades. Combine the emulator with another container An external dependency needs an engine’s behavior, such as PostgreSQL for migrations or ORM queries. Run another service on the test machine or runner. An engine container covers database behavior within its setup, while deployed RDS configuration still needs its own checks. In the build Isenberg tested, emulated Cognito issued ES256-signed tokens while the live Cognito flow used by the suite expected RS256. The reported user pool scenario also did not invoke Lambda triggers. A local token fixture kept the application scenarios runnable and left the live Cognito behavior to end-to-end tests. Isenberg discusses using a real PostgreSQL engine in a separate container as an option for relational workloads. The Cookbook uses DynamoDB, so the PostgreSQL approach was outside the reported experiment. Trade-offs in the original article
When a difference appears, start with the purpose of the test. A failure fixture may be enough when the question is how the application reacts. When the question is whether an AWS service actually behaves that way, record which AWS check provides the evidence. That makes the cost of each workaround visible when the test suite changes.
6. Reading Compatibility Evidence by Release The author recorded 6,908 reports in the known-gaps directory on November 12, 2026. This number describes the repository at the time of the review. For a project decision, check whether the specific operations and failure cases your application uses are covered. A broad service label or score can hide differences between managing a resource and using its data plane. The author’s observations
Amazon describes three groups of agents behind the original project. One group develops reference tests using AWS. Another identifies differences in the emulator. The third fixes those differences and submits changes through automated checks. Isenberg raised a question about public visibility of the tests. AWS documentation now points to the public AWS Emulator Evaluation Suite and explains how fidelity scores relate to releases. Compare scores against the same version of the evaluation suite when judging changes. How Amazon built AWS Emulator · AWS guidance on fidelity · Evaluation Suite repository
7. Evaluating the Emulator for Another Repository Inventory the AWS calls. Read the application code, CDK or Terraform configuration, and existing tests. Identify the data-plane calls and deployment behavior each test depends on. Try a small representative path. Run one integration case from the handler through the SDK to an emulated resource. Record the emulator version, endpoint, fixtures, and observed behavior. Use sample data and emulator-only credentials. Record the coverage boundary. For each mock or workaround, state what the local test covers and which AWS test verifies the remaining behavior. Keep a controlled E2E path from the client to deployed services. Revisit the result after updates. Run the same tests against a new emulator version and compare against the expected AWS contract. Remove a workaround once the relevant project scenario passes with the standard path. The author packaged this evaluation into an AWS Emulator adoption skill. It inventories application and infrastructure dependencies, checks relevant operations locally, and produces a report of compatibility and workarounds. The Cookbook’s emulator configuration is a second reference for teams planning a similar trial. AWS Emulator adoption skill · Cookbook emulator configuration
For the Cookbook, the emulator made the integration loop faster because the core tests exercised application code against sufficiently compatible DynamoDB operations. A useful test record names the layers each result actually covered. Local checks surface application issues early, and the deployed suite verifies the configuration and access controls the application will use on AWS.

title: Event 3
content:
First Cloud AI Journey Meetup Date · Saturday, October 24, 2026 Time · 09:00–12:00 (UTC+7) Venue · 26th floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Organizer · First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Role · In-person attendee Event objectives The meetup offered five practical perspectives on building and operating applications on AWS. The talks ranged from real-time Vietnamese conversations to cross-account resource sharing, pre-release security reviews, and context management for AI agents. I was especially interested in the decisions behind the demonstrations, such as how to measure what a user experiences and how much access an agent needs for a given task.
Speakers and program Session Topic Speakers 1 Hear, Think, Speak – Building a Vietnamese Voice AI Contact Center on AWS Kiệt Trần · Revve AI 2 AWS Resource Access Manager Long Huỳnh · Styl Solution 3 AWS Pentest with AWS Continuum / Security Agent Thịnh Nguyễn · Styl Solution 4 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Xuân An · Leader, AWS Student Builder Group HCMUTE 5 Kiro Crew Khoa Kiều · Tech Lead, ACB. Nghi Danh · AWS Community Builder Key highlights Session 1 · A Vietnamese voice AI contact center on AWS Kiệt Trần explained a conversational turn through three stages: Hear, Think, Speak. The system receives speech, processes its meaning, and responds with speech. In a phone call, the gap between the end of a sentence and the start of the reply directly affects how the exchange feels. The session cited about 1.8 seconds in the context of the solution discussed at the meetup.
The most memorable example was a live call simulating an initial screening interview for a Cloud Engineer role in Vietnamese. Hearing questions and answers over the phone made the effect of response time tangible. A similar test could measure the delay while also checking whether questions are clear, whether follow-ups fit the conversation, and whether the person on the other end can follow the exchange.
Session 2 · Sharing resources with AWS Resource Access Manager Long Huỳnh covered how to share supported resources across accounts in AWS Organizations using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). A networking account can, for example, share subnets where application accounts deploy their own resources. This lets a team manage the network centrally and avoid recreating components that the accounts can share. AWS RAM
I took three questions from the session. Which resource is shared, and with which account? Which actions do IAM policies grant to users or roles in the receiving account? What maximum permissions does the service control policy (SCP) set for the member account? Looking at the three together explains why different teams can have different access to the same shared resource. AWS RAM and SCPs
Session 3 · Pre-release security reviews with AWS Security Agent Thịnh Nguyễn discussed how AWS Security Agent, part of AWS Continuum, can bring security review earlier into development. Examples included reviewing Terraform infrastructure changes and surfacing findings in GitHub pull requests or GitLab merge requests. Developers can examine a finding alongside the relevant change and review the proposed fix before merging. AWS Security Agent code review
The session also discussed security assessments on SIT/UAT environments within an approved scope before release. The two checkpoints I took away were the review of the proposed change and the confirmation of the fix in a test environment. A team can track a finding from the first report through verification by the person responsible for the change.
Discussion about application security before deployment.
Session 4 · Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and Memory Xuân An described two components involved in operating an agent. AgentCore Runtime provides its execution environment. In the microVM model shown, each session has its own environment with isolated memory and filesystem resources. The temporary state in that environment supports interactions during the active session. AgentCore Runtime microVMs
AgentCore Memory helps an application decide which information to retain. Short-term memory stores interactions as events so the agent can continue the current conversation. With a long-term memory strategy, the service can asynchronously extract and consolidate useful information for later sessions. That distinction leads to a concrete design choice about which data needs to be available for the next turn and which can be processed in the background. AgentCore memory types
The Runtime presentation illustrated microVM isolation and temporary state for each session.
Session 5 · Kiro Crew Khoa Kiều and Nghi Danh presented Kiro Crew for background tasks such as supporting code review and checking system health. This was my favorite session because the Q&A addressed practical issues that come up when an agent becomes part of everyday work.
Artifacts. The demo aggregated job listing data and presented statistics as a chart inside the chat. A visual result made it easier to review the output, especially when the criteria used to summarize the data were clear. Context window. The discussion covered Auto Compact thresholds around 70–90% and using Break down context to see which components use the most tokens. Compaction condenses earlier history in a long session. Kiro’s documentation lists 70% as the configurable default. Kiro Crew session context Memory and guardrails. The speakers discussed reviewing older memory entries, retaining information that still serves a purpose, and controlling agent actions. For a system health task, I can define what the agent may read, require approval for infrastructure changes, and limit access to secrets and credentials. Kiro Crew tool permissions A speaker and attendees during the technical Q&A.
Key takeaways Measure the user’s experience. For a voice assistant, the time until a reply starts is a useful first measure. I also need to check the clarity of the reply and whether it fits the conversation. Review sharing and permissions together. When several teams use a common network component, I need to identify the owning account, the participating accounts, and the scope of each team’s actions. Match data retention to the task. An agent continuing the current conversation needs different information from one interacting with the same user in a later session. The purpose and retention period should guide what gets stored in memory. Make outputs easy for other people to verify. A review finding or chart is easier to assess when the reader can trace it to the relevant change or source data. Applying the ideas to work For the PDF-to-profile feature in the Tindy proposal, I can measure the time from submitting a request to seeing the draft and check individual fields against sample documents. The interface can show which step is pending and which fields still need user confirmation. This applies the measurement idea from the voice AI demo to a task with a concrete result in Tindy.
In the team’s review workflow, I can use an agent to summarize a change, identify points for review, and link to the relevant documentation. The person responsible for the change can verify those observations before deciding what to fix or merge. The quality of each review comment provides a practical way to evaluate that use of an agent.
Event experience The morning at Bitexco gave me a chance to hear tech leads and engineers describe problems they encounter when applying cloud and AI in their work. The Vietnamese screening call and the Kiro Crew Q&A stood out. The call showed me what delay feels like to the listener, while the discussion helped me understand why a background agent needs focused context and clear permissions.
I appreciate the speakers and organizers for giving students a chance to learn from real examples and ask questions. The meetup encouraged me to approach people in the community and bring more specific questions to future events.
