The program followed AI across the engineering lifecycle, from defining requirements and building an application to testing, modernizing code, and operating a system. The morning focused on decisions teams face when putting AI into use. The afternoon offered two parallel workshops with AWS Solutions Architects and a case study from Kyanon Digital.
Speakers Speaker Role Program contribution Nguyen Gia Hung Head of Solutions Architect for Vietnam and Cambodia Welcome, workshop briefing, and Customer Spotlight moderation Dzung Ha Solutions Architect Taking agentic AI from demo to deployment Binh Tran Senior Solutions Architect Building data products for AI agents Taiki Dang Solutions Architect Code modernization with AWS Transform Nhut Le Solutions Architect Workshop A on building an application with Kiro Thi Nguyen Solutions Architect Workshop B on deploying an AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Bui Hoang Viet DevOps Engineer, Kyanon Digital Customer Spotlight on limiting the impact of LLM-assisted remediation in Kubernetes Full agenda Time (UTC+7) Activity Speaker or organization 09:15–09:30 Welcome Address Nguyen Gia Hung 09:30–10:10 From Demo to Deployment: Solving Agentic AI’s Toughest Challenges Dzung Ha, with a customer contribution from Katalon 10:10–10:50 Building High-Quality Data Products for AI Agents Binh Tran 10:50–11:15 Networking break — 11:15–11:55 Migration at Scale with AWS Transform Taiki Dang 11:55–12:15 Workshop briefing and track selection Nguyen Gia Hung 12:15–13:15 Buffet lunch at the hotel restaurant — 13:15–15:15 Workshop A · Build with Kiro: From Spec to Working Application Nhut Le 13:15–15:15 Workshop B · Build & Deploy AI Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore using Vibe Coding with Kiro Thi Nguyen 15:15–15:35 Afternoon break — 15:35–16:15 Customer Spotlight · Beyond Single-YAML: Taming the Blast Radius of LLM Remediation in Kubernetes Bui Hoang Viet, Nguyen Gia Hung 16:30–18:00 Networking drinks at Hai Bar Sam Williams Key highlights Welcome and taking agentic AI from demo to deployment Nguyen Gia Hung opened the day by introducing the connections between application development, data, modernization, and operations. The examples were aimed at engineering teams that want to understand the steps involved in bringing an AI feature into a product.
Welcome address in the main event room.
Dzung Ha then covered four issues engineering teams face when moving from an agent demo to a deployed system.
Operations. Teams need ways to observe errors, latency, and the step where a request gets stuck. Data governance. Agents need defined data sources, clear ownership, and appropriate access. Reliability. Testing should cover routine requests and cases where a tool or data source fails to return what the agent expects. Trust. Users and engineering teams need to understand what supports an output and when it needs further review. The Katalon True Platform example applied this thinking to software quality. Katalon described an AWS-based platform that uses test results and quality data to verify changes produced with AI. When an agent changes a feature, test history and execution results give reviewers evidence they can use to check that the feature still behaves as intended. Katalon True Platform
Building data products for AI agents Binh Tran focused on three aspects of an agent’s inputs: data quality, schema design, and keeping data current through real-time integration. When several systems use the same data product, field names, types, and status definitions need to be clear enough for developers and agents to interpret consistently.
I related this to tracking a document processing request. A data product could define states such as pending, complete, and failed, together with the time of the last update. The agent can use those fields to report the current state, and the application can compare the output with the source system.
Modernizing code at scale with AWS Transform Taiki Dang presented AWS Transform through examples that included upgrading Java, modernizing .NET, migrating frameworks, and addressing technical debt. The process discussed starts with describing the intended result, defining the scope, applying changes, and validating the result. That approach is useful when the same kind of change needs to be repeated across repositories. AWS Transform custom · Modernizing .NET
My takeaway was to decide what evidence would support the transformation. Before changing a runtime version or framework, a team can record build and test results as a baseline. After the change, it can compare behavior, identify dependencies that still need attention, and decide which repositories or components to migrate next.
Parallel afternoon workshops Both tracks ran from 13:15 to 15:15. The event instructions asked attendees to bring a laptop and prepare an AWS Builder ID if their track required it. The same identity could be used to continue using Kiro after the session. AWS Builder ID
Workshop A · Build an application with Kiro. Nhut Le’s track guided participants from a description of the application to three deliverables drafted by Kiro: requirements, a design, and implementation tasks. Participants could refine acceptance criteria, guide individual tasks, try the resulting application, and revise any gaps. Kiro Specs
Workshop B · Build and deploy an AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Thi Nguyen’s track started with an agent built using Kiro and moved it to the cloud with AgentCore. The agenda described adding capabilities after getting the first version running. It raised practical questions about where an agent executes, which tools it may call, and what to watch once it is deployed. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore overview
Customer Spotlight · Limiting the impact of changes in Kubernetes Bui Hoang Viet, a DevOps Engineer at Kyanon Digital, spoke about using LLMs to support proposed remediation for Kubernetes incidents. The Beyond Single-YAML topic asks how one configuration change could affect the running workload and related components. For example, a team needs to understand which workload is affected, which settings are shared, and how to restore an earlier configuration if the system responds unexpectedly.
I took away the need to trace a proposal through to the deployment decision. A team can review the change, exercise it in a test environment, and use the same health signals to compare behavior before and after a release.
Key takeaways Use test results as review evidence. I can connect a change to its acceptance criteria, test cases, and execution results. This gives the team something concrete to review when AI contributes code. Define the input data before evaluating an agent. A clear schema, field definitions, and data freshness expectations help the team locate whether an unexpected result comes from the source data or the agent’s processing. Keep the scope of a change small enough to verify. When modernizing code or changing infrastructure configuration, a team can check one part at a time and record how to restore a known version. Define operating criteria while prototyping. An AI feature benefits from an explicit definition of a correct result, a way to measure processing time, and signals to consult when a run fails. Applying the ideas to work For the PDF-to-profile feature in the Tindy proposal, I can specify what PDF input to accept, which fields to extract, and how to display missing information. A set of sample documents gives the team a way to test each extracted field. The pull request can include test evidence so reviewers can check the change against the spec.
The Customer Spotlight also gave me a way to think about the impact of changes in Tindy. Before altering the configuration of a document-processing worker, I can list its queues and dependencies, check the change in a test environment, and review document status and failure rates after release. The rollout plan can include how to restore the previous settings.

The progression from data and testing to deployment helped me connect AI with specific engineering tasks in my project. title: Runtime, seeding and Edge
content:
Connect the deployed stacks into a running Tindy environment. Edge provides the HTTPS hostname. Runtime runs the API behind CloudFront VPC Origin and an internal ALB. Database tasks prepare DB roles, schema and demo data before enabling the API.
Keep Edge in maintenance and Runtime at DesiredCount 0 while preparing secrets, bootstrap, migrations and seed data. Open traffic after successful DB tasks and API health checks.
5.5.1 — Create Edge in maintenance mode Create edge.yaml first to obtain DistributionDomainName, used as Runtime CloudFrontPublicHost and for OAuth callback updates during authentication verification.
Component Purpose CloudFront distribution Provides the HTTPS entry point for frontend and API. Origin Access Control Enables CloudFront access to the frontend S3 origin through its bucket policy. Frontend bucket policy Restricts origin access to the configured distribution. Maintenance routing function Returns HTTP 503 and maintenance JSON for API routes while the backend is being prepared. Initially use EdgeMode = maintenance and leave AlbDnsName and VpcOriginId empty. Switch to live with the new Runtime values after the API becomes healthy.
Expected result is CREATE_COMPLETE, three Outputs and HTTPS /api/health/ready returning HTTP 503 with maintenance JSON.
5.5.2 — Create Runtime with DesiredCount zero runtime.yaml consumes inputs from Foundation, Network, Database, Integrations and Edge.
Resource group Purpose ECS cluster, task definition and service Define the image, configuration, secret references, CPU/memory and task count. Execution and task IAM roles Support container startup and application AWS access. Internal ALB, listener and target group Receive VPC Origin traffic, route requests to the container and check health. CloudFront VPC Origin Connects the distribution to the internal ALB. Security group ingress Restricts ALB access according to CloudFront configuration. CloudWatch log group Records API and database task logs. Conditional one-off task definitions Run bootstrap, migrations and seeding once required parameters are supplied. Create Runtime with a digest-pinned image, DBProvisionMode = Fresh and DesiredCount = 0. Retain the verified OAuth, media and Bedrock text settings. Keep AI PDF false during schema preparation. Once the zero-count service exists, prepare secrets and update parameters to enable DB tasks.
Stages after Runtime creation Order Work Verification 1 Prepare application/migration/seed secrets and verify the new endpoint. content:

Where Should You Start? My talk on starting with AWS and choosing resources for different learning goals. 10:00–10:25 AWS Lambda Web Functions: Rethinking Serverless Web Architecture Native HTTP, concurrent request processing, and evaluating performance and cost. 10:30–11:00 Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems Decoupling producers and workers with queues, and comparing Standard and FIFO. 11:00–11:25 My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey An FCAJ internship and a serverless card game project. 11:30–12:00 Start & Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing Making a first contribution and developing a consistent contribution habit. Key highlights Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories Henry Duc Bui, Head of Engineering at CloudThinker, shared lessons from applying AI-DLC to the team’s software development process. He showed a monthly chart of merges into the develop branch as an example of how the team tracked its workflow. For me, a metric like this raises follow-up questions about review time, what kinds of changes are merged, and how the team assesses quality. Henry Duc Bui’s session introduction
Opening talk on CloudThinker's experience building software factories. My talk · New to AWS? Where Should You Start? In the Education session, I opened with a question about where to start when there are many places to learn AWS. I introduced three resources by the purpose each one serves. This gives students a concrete way to choose their next step, whether that is to learn a concept, complete a workshop, or see how other builders approach a similar problem.
Resource What I introduced AWS Study Group Step-by-step workshops, including Vietnamese materials, for practicing how to configure and check AWS resources. AWS Skill Builder Topic-based courses, labs, and certification preparation for structured learning. AWS Builder Center Community articles and workshops, student activities, and badge opportunities subject to the relevant program requirements. AWS Skill Builder · AWS Builder Center
My explanation of the purpose of each AWS learning resource. I used these resources to connect classroom learning with engineering work. A student can learn a concept in a module, verify it with a small lab, and capture the result in a diagram, a screenshot, or a short explanation. When the concept comes up in a project, that record helps explain which service was chosen, how it was tested, and what could be done differently next time.
The talk also mentioned opportunities to explore AWS credits. For a new learner, that is a reason to check the eligibility conditions and get into the habit of tracking costs during the first labs.
AWS Lambda Web Functions and serverless web architecture The session covered running an application as a native HTTP server on Lambda Web Functions. An application can use a supported Node.js web framework without an adapter specific to Lambda event payloads. A single execution environment can handle multiple requests at the same time. 128 requests is the maximum configurable concurrency per environment. Lambda adjusts the actual limit based on resource usage and load. Lambda Web Functions · Scaling behavior
The session discussed Active CPU Billing and used live benchmarks to compare this model with container-based applications on EC2 and ECS. Web Functions charges include requests, active CPU time, memory over the environment’s lifetime, and data transfer. When interpreting a benchmark, I would compare the shape of the workload, initialization latency, and how much time requests spend waiting for I/O. Execution and billing model
The talk compared how Lambda handles concurrent traffic. Amazon SQS and asynchronous processing The Amazon SQS session showed how a queue separates a producer from a worker. The producer can finish accepting the request, while workers process queued messages at a rate the downstream system can handle. The two sides can scale more independently as the amount of work changes.
The diagram at the venue compared Standard and FIFO queues. Standard queues deliver at least once and can deliver out of order. FIFO preserves order within a message group and supports send deduplication. A useful test is to see whether a worker can receive the same job again without repeating a write or changing the job to an incorrect state. SQS Standard · SQS FIFO
Comparing delivery behavior and message ordering for the two queue types. My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey Khang Duong described a three-month internship at FCAJ through the example of building a serverless card game on AWS. The talk connected learning individual services to using them in a project. For students preparing for an internship, it showed one way to explain the experience through implementation steps and lessons from the work.
The internship talk connected AWS services with project work. Starting and sustaining open source contributions The last session covered finding a first contribution and continuing once the workflow becomes familiar. A small change such as improving a guide or clarifying an issue can teach a newcomer how to read project conventions, communicate with maintainers, and respond to review. My takeaway was to treat each contribution as an example of a problem I investigated and a result I improved.
Closing session on developing a consistent open source contribution habit. What I learned as a speaker Start with the audience’s question. For a student new to AWS, asking where to start leads to a concrete action, such as choosing a topic and using a lab to check their understanding. Explain the purpose before introducing the tool. Presenting each learning resource through a specific need makes it easier to remember when to use it. Use examples and evidence when describing what I learned. I can explain a lab or project through its original requirement, what I did, what I observed, and what still needs testing. Applying the ideas to work The SQS session relates to the document-processing flow in the Tindy proposal. One test can deliver a PDF scan event more than once and check that the worker updates the document status consistently. I can keep the result with the flow diagram so that the queue’s role is easy to explain when presenting the project.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Overall evaluation Working and learning environment What I valued about FCAJ was the opportunity to learn in several ways. I could study AWS fundamentals by topic and hear engineering teams describe how they use those services at work. The Amazon SQS session at Community Day, for example, provided a practical example to connect with the queuing concepts in my worklog. Speaking at the event also gave me a reason to organize what I had learned for a beginner audience.
Mentor and program coordinator support The most useful form of support for a project intern is feedback on a specific deliverable. A review of Tindy’s architecture could focus on how a request flows through the system, where data is stored, and how the team can verify the flow. At the deployment milestone, a similar review could focus on a pull request, an integration issue, or a post-release check. Keeping support times and question channels in one place would help interns prepare material and use mentor time effectively.
Relevance to my major Tindy gave me a way to connect my information technology coursework with a system that uses a frontend, API, PostgreSQL, and AWS components. Each implementation decision also raised questions about access, environment configuration, observability, and recovery. For example, the PDF scanning workflow needs to explain both how users see the document status and how the worker handles failed messages.
Learning and skill development The program gave me opportunities to practice technical research and communication. I selected articles on Kiro Workflows, AgentCore, and AWS Emulator and summarized them for the report. Preparing the Community Day Education session required me to explain a learning path at a level suited to beginners. Organizing AWS Study Group, AWS Skill Builder, and AWS Builder Center by purpose helped turn the resources I had explored into a guide people could follow.
Knowledge sharing and teamwork I valued hearing both practitioners and community members speak at FCAJ events. The format gives interns a place to bring their questions and share what they have learned. In project work, I want to keep updates short and concrete by reporting what is complete, what is blocked, and which changes affect others. That gives frontend, backend, and infrastructure contributors an early signal when they need to coordinate.
Resources and hands-on access Workshops, learning materials, and community events helped me plan what to study. For labs that require account access or provision resources, it would help to state which environment to use, what permissions are needed, what support or credit eligibility is available where applicable, and how to clean up. Interns would then be better prepared to start the lab and check its impact on their budget afterward.
What I appreciated most My highlight was presenting New to AWS? Where Should You Start? at FCAJ Community Day. I used resources I had explored to answer a question students often ask. I would recommend FCAJ to students who want a structured way to study AWS, practice through a project, and participate in a community. If I have the opportunity to stay involved, I would like to share a short lab or help new learners choose resources that match their goals.
Suggestions for future cohorts Provide one place to start in the first week. An onboarding page could bring together the weekly plan, learning links, deliverable expectations, question channels, and examples of evidence to capture. A new module could point to a short lab and a question students can use to check their understanding. Hold a short technical review at the end of each sprint. A team could bring an architecture diagram, pull request, or demo recording. The team and mentor could agree on one thing to verify before the next sprint. This would help surface access, data, or deployment issues sooner. Include an operations exercise before the deployment milestone. A short exercise could start with API 5xx errors and work through ALB target health, ECS events, and application logs. The output could record an observation, a hypothesis, and a verification step so interns have a model for documenting troubleshooting. Keep short speaking opportunities open to interns. A five- to ten-minute session in a small group could cover a lab, an architecture decision, or a problem someone investigated. This would give more interns a chance to practice before speaking at a larger event such as Community Day.
